newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Kia troubles hit already struggling S.Korean banks.
newsitem.headline: Kia troubles hit already struggling S.Korean banks.

text.p: The Kia Group's financial crisis is likely to deal an additional blow to South Korean banks, already struggling in the aftermath of a string of corporate failures, analysts said on Wednesday.

"The bail-out decision is to prevent a bankruptcy, but people will simply think it's a de facto bankruptcy," said Kim Min-tae, an analyst at the LG Economic Research Institute. "So the impact on banks will be as serious as a bankruptcy would have been."

One of Kia's main creditor banks, the Korea First Bank, announced on Tuesday that Kia Motors Corp and 17 of the group's other 38 affiliates would be rescued under a scheme formed in April by financial institutions.
"It's hard to estimate damages in numbers, but banks will see funding costs soaring and borrowing chances decreasing in international markets," said Park So-young, an analyst at Daewoo Securities.
On the Seoul stock market, bank shares plunged for the second day on Wednesday, with the banking sub-index shedding 5.8 percent following a 2.0 percent drop on Tuesday.
Analysts said the Korea First Bank was expected to be hit hardest, particularly since it was also the main creditor to the stricken Hanbo Group.
Korea First shares fell 280 won to their limit of 3,220 won. It had 1.53 trillion won ($1.7 billion) in outstanding loans to Kia, whose debts totalled 9.54 trillion at the end of May.
The Hanbo Group's flagship Hanbo Steel Co was declared insolvent in January with debts of 6.6 trillion won.

Its failure rippled through the economy, already battered by slowing exports and a cyclical downturn, and was followed two months later by the collapse of leading stainless steel products maker, Sammi Steel Co.
"The Kia Group has more debts than Hanbo, but Kia did not go bankrupt. Therefore, losses of banks could be small if the group overcomes its current crisis," said Park of Daewoo.
If Kia manages to stay afloat, banks would not have to build up huge reserves to cover non-performing loans as they are required to do when their clients fold, she said.
Analysts said Kia would probably be broken up and sold off to other conglomerates.

"Banks will have to endure some loss by offering favourable debt servicing conditions to help the takeover be realised," said Park of Daewoo. "But it would be far less than the loss they would have to suffer if Kia goes bankrupt."
Lee Jung-ja, head of research at HSBC James Capel, said the takeover of Kia would take some time and the banking sector in the meantime would have to pour money into Kia.
Analysts said Kia's troubles underscored the lack of advanced credit analysis practices in the local financial industry.
Kia had total liabilities of 11.89 trillion won at the end of 1996, more than five times shareholders' equity of 2.27 trillion, Office of Bank Supervision statistics show.
"If banks kept loans to a company within an appropriate level in terms of the company's net worth, the impact from any single bankruptcy would be easily digested," said Kim of LG.
